script.opening: “The hospital says the cameras were all clear, which is good I suppose. But I’m still shattered, I get puffed on the stairs, and those iron tablets made me so ill I stopped them.”

facts.text: Tired all the time, breathless on the stairs, a bit dizzy on standing. No chest pain. No visible blood loss: no blood in stools or urine, no vomiting blood. Postmenopausal for 15 years, no vaginal bleeding. Weight steady.
Ferrous sulfate once a day for three weeks. Felt sick, constipated, and her stools went black. Stopped them a month ago. Took them with breakfast and a cup of tea.
Black but formed, not sticky or tarry, no unusual smell, and they returned to brown within days of stopping the tablets. No black stools since.
Little red meat, lots of tea. Ibuprofen from the supermarket most days for her back for about a year. No aspirin or anticoagulants. Amlodipine for BP.

Her friend Pat had a clear colonoscopy and was diagnosed with bowel cancer a year later. Sheila thinks the cameras might have missed something, and the black stools “proved it”. Also read online that iron drips can cause a severe allergic reaction.
Cares for Brian, 72, with Parkinson’s; he falls if left long. Daughter helps one afternoon a week. Tired from broken nights.

Matter-of-fact, slightly apologetic about stopping the tablets. Relieved when the black stools are explained. Becomes anxious about the iron drip until the risk is put in proportion; then practical about arranging cover for Brian.

ice.ideas: “I’m just anaemic and tired from looking after Brian.”

ice.expectations: “Something for the tiredness that doesn’t make me ill.”

checkpoints.text: Reviews the results and investigations so far (persistent iron deficiency after normal gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies, colonoscopy, coeliac serology and urinalysis) and asks about symptoms and ongoing blood loss
Clarifies the black stools (formed, not tarry, resolved after stopping iron) and distinguishes iron-darkened stools from melaena
Identifies contributors: daily over-the-counter ibuprofen, tea with iron, diet

Manages oral iron intolerance: once-daily or alternate-day dosing, an alternative preparation, taken with vitamin C and away from tea, coffee and antacids (check the SPC/local formulary), with a recheck of Hb after about 2–4 weeks
Explains intravenous iron as an option if oral iron is not tolerated or does not work, with honest information that serious reactions are rare and are managed by the infusion team
Stops the ibuprofen and offers safer analgesia for her back

Explains when further investigation is needed (if anaemia persists or recurs despite adequate iron, refer back to gastroenterology for consideration of small-bowel investigation) and addresses her fear that cancer was missed with honest, proportionate information
Explores her concerns and caring situation, arranges practical cover for appointments, and safety-nets (melaena, rectal bleeding, worsening breathlessness or chest pain, weight loss)

worked.txt: “The cameras looked at your stomach, the first part of your small bowel and your whole large bowel, and they were clear, as were the coeliac test and the urine. That’s genuinely reassuring. But you’re still low on iron, so we need to fix that and keep an eye on why.”

“Iron tablets often turn stools very dark or black. The worrying kind of black stool is sticky, tarry and smells awful. Yours were formed and went back to normal when you stopped the tablets. That fits the iron.”
“You said the clear result was good ‘I suppose’. Is part of you worried they’ve missed something?”
“Taking iron every other day is often just as effective and much easier on the stomach. Take it with orange juice, not tea, and away from indigestion remedies.”
“If tablets don’t work, an iron drip in hospital is very effective. Serious allergic reactions are rare, and the team watch you closely and know exactly what to do.”

“If your iron keeps falling despite treatment, I’d send you back to the bowel team to look at the small bowel, which the standard cameras don’t reach. That’s a planned next step, not a sign anything was missed.”

f.learning: Iron-deficiency anaemia in a postmenopausal woman needs investigation for gastrointestinal blood loss and malabsorption: the BSG guideline (2021) recommends coeliac serology, urinalysis and bidirectional endoscopy (gastroscopy with duodenal biopsies and colonoscopy) for most, and NICE NG12 includes IDA in suspected cancer pathway criteria. When these are negative, the next steps are to replace iron effectively and monitor. Oral iron causes gastrointestinal side effects in many people; once-daily or alternate-day dosing improves tolerance and can maintain absorption because of hepcidin effects, and absorption improves with vitamin C and worsens with tea, coffee, calcium and antacids (check the SPC/local formulary). Recheck Hb after 2–4 weeks; a rise of about 20 g/L over 3–4 weeks shows a good response. Intravenous iron is indicated when oral iron is not tolerated or is ineffective; serious hypersensitivity reactions are rare and infusions are given where resuscitation facilities are available. Iron commonly darkens stools; melaena is black, tarry, sticky and offensive, and needs urgent assessment. Remove contributors such as NSAIDs. If IDA persists or recurs despite adequate replacement after negative bidirectional endoscopy, refer back to gastroenterology for consideration of small-bowel investigation (for example capsule endoscopy), and reconsider non-GI causes. The consultation skill is uncovering the fear that cancer was missed, giving honest reassurance about what the tests did and did not show, and making the plan workable for a carer who cannot easily leave home.

model.text: Hello Mrs Drummond, I’m Dr Clarke. How are you getting on since the hospital tests?
The hospital says the cameras were all clear, which is good I suppose. But I’m still shattered, I get puffed on the stairs, and those iron tablets made me so ill I stopped them.
I’m sorry they made you ill. What happened with the tablets?
Sick, bunged up, and my stools went black. That frightened me. I stopped after three weeks.
Can you describe the black stools? Were they sticky or tarry, did they smell much worse than usual, and did they go back to normal after you stopped?
Just black, normal otherwise. Back to brown within a few days of stopping.
Any blood in your stools or urine, vomiting blood, chest pain, or weight loss?
No, nothing like that.
How did you take the tablets, and do you take anything else, like painkillers from the shop?
With breakfast and a cup of tea. And ibuprofen most days for my back.
You said the clear result was good ‘I suppose’. Is part of you worried they missed something?
(pause) My friend Pat had a clear camera test and got bowel cancer a year later. When my stools went black I thought, there it is.
That must have been frightening, especially after Pat. Thank you for telling me. Let me explain what the tests did show and what the black stools were.

The cameras looked at your stomach, the start of your small bowel and the whole of your large bowel, and took samples, and the coeliac and urine tests were clear. That’s genuinely reassuring. And iron tablets turn stools black; the worrying kind is sticky and tarry. Yours fit the iron.

No test is perfect, so here’s the safety net: if your iron keeps dropping despite treatment, I’ll send you back to the bowel team to look at the part of the small bowel the standard cameras can’t reach.
model.why: Honest limits; threshold for further investigation

model.text: For the iron: let’s try a tablet every other day, which is often just as effective and much easier on the stomach. Take it with orange juice, not tea, and keep tea an hour or two away. I’d stop the ibuprofen, as it can cause slow bleeding from the stomach, and we’ll find something safer for your back.
And if that doesn’t work?

Then an iron drip in hospital, which works very well. I know you’ve read about reactions. Serious ones are rare, and the team watches you and knows exactly what to do. It would take a couple of hours, so we’d plan cover for Brian, perhaps on your daughter’s afternoon.
That would work. She comes on Thursdays.
Can you tell me the plan?
Iron every other day with orange juice, not tea. No ibuprofen. Blood test in a few weeks. Drip if it doesn’t work. Back to the bowel team if it keeps dropping.

Exactly. Blood test in three weeks. If you get black, sticky, tarry stools, blood from your back passage, worse breathlessness, chest pain or fainting, get help the same day. And would a carer’s assessment be helpful? You’ve a lot on.
